entries.title: The Best Nonfiction Books of 2026: The Baillie Gifford Prize Shortlist, recommended by Kirsty Lang
entries.summary: “'Tis strange—but true; for truth is always strange; stranger than fiction,” wrote Lord Byron. For more than a quarter of a century, the Baillie Gifford Prize has celebrated the best nonfiction book of the year. Broadcaster Kirsty Lang, chair of this year's judging panel, talks us through the six books shortlisted for the 2026 prize, from Alexander the Great to Barbara Cartland. This interview app
entries.content:
For those who haven’t come across it, could you introduce the Baillie Gifford Prize and explain what kind of books you’re looking for as judges?

The Baillie Gifford Prize is one of the most important nonfiction book prizes in the English language. It was formerly known as the Samuel Johnson Prize, and has been going since 1999.

What the judges are looking for is good narrative nonfiction. It must be nonfiction with a literary quality, rather than, say, a very academic book. It should have evidence of original research, and a copy-and-paste job will not do.

So it’s got to be original, readable, and have wide appeal. But by wide appeal, I don’t mean dumbing down. We have some very smart books on the list.

The prize rewards quality narrative nonfiction. It should read like a good novel, but be true.

Let’s go through the books that have been shortlisted for the 2026 prize. Can we start with the one that goes furthest back in time? This is Alexander: God, King, and Man by Edmund Richardson. This is a biography of Alexander the Great, but written a bit like fiction. Tell me more.

Everybody who’s rushing to read Homer’s Odyssey after the Christopher Nolan film will love this book. Although Edmund Richardson is a professor of classics at Durham University, he’s written it so it’s very immersive—like a cinematic page-turner. It reminded me of those old-fashioned sword-and-sandal films. You feel that you’re there watching these people.

At the same time, it’s packed with new research. He drew on source material from about a dozen ancient languages. He then uses modern technology to cross-reference and do data analysis. This allows him to go into amazing details like, ‘Given the supply chains, would they have been hungry?’ ‘How hot would it have been? Landscapes have changed –  would they be marching through desert or would it have been savanna?’ You get a real sense of the landscape.

It’s also a fascinating lesson in leadership. Alexander was really young, and he persuaded thousands of men to march into unknown lands across thousands of miles—from ancient Macedon, through ancient Greece, Egypt. He pursued the Persian king, Darius, right across Persia into India.

They didn’t have maps; they didn’t know where they were going—they believed they were going to fall off the existing world. How did Alexander persuade people to follow him? Edward Richardson says he was a great storyteller and had a good story to tell about why they should keep following him and conquering lands. He also doesn’t flinch from Alexander’s brutality.

Yes, I was going to ask: what picture of Alexander emerges from the book?

You spend quite a lot of time wondering what motivates him. In the beginning, he’s broke. He inherits a country where the coffers are empty. Initially, it’s a moneymaking expedition. You conquer and you plunder and everybody gets rich. But there’s a certain point in his travels where he could have said, ‘We’re all rich enough now, we can go home.’ But he doesn’t. He carries on. I came to the conclusion that Alexander was good at battles and less good at ruling because ruling is boring—people moaning about paying taxes or not having water etc. He liked a good battle.

Let’s turn to another book on the 2026 shortlist. What can you tell me about Baldwin: A Love Story by Nicholas Boggs?

This is the first biography of James Baldwin in 30 years. He was a very important figure in the civil rights movement and a very good writer of both fiction and nonfiction. Baldwin is having another moment because he was a very good public speaker. A lot of his speeches and debates with right-wing racists are now emerging again on YouTube, so a new generation is discovering him.

It’s the first biography to look at Baldwin through the prism of his love life. It’s divided into four sections, and each one is about one of the four most important loves of Baldwin’s life. I was a little bit sceptical at first because I thought, ‘Are you therefore reducing him? Are you just focusing on him as a gay man?’ But, actually, what Boggs explains is that a lot of Baldwin’s ideas about race, about masculinity, about gender, were all intertwined. He argued that America’s racial problems were tied up with this myth of white American masculinity—your John Waynes and your Charlton Hestons.

I mention Charlton Heston because one of the stories in the book that I was most surprised by is that at a certain point, Columbia Pictures hired Baldwin to write a script about the life of Malcolm X. They suggested to him that Charlton Heston might be a good candidate to play the role, blacked up.

The book is relevant now, post-Black Lives Matter. A lot of people are disappointed with the rise of white supremacy and racism in the United States, the continuing violence against African American men, and are rediscovering James Baldwin.

Boggs also writes really well. Again, it doesn’t sanctify Baldwin. It shows his blemishes. Like a lot of artists and writers, he was brilliant, but he was also quite selfish and self-obsessed. When it comes to gender, he’s not perfect around feminism by any means. He had strong female friendships and there’s quite a shocking passage where a female friend shares the fact that she has been sexually molested by somebody. The response in his letter almost brushes over it.

But, towards the end of his life, you can see that his views around gender are shifting. He writes a lot about androgyny and how all of us contain some male and some female. He also writes about how we all contain black and white, as we are all descended from Africans.

Then there is Baldwin’s message of love—that the only way you can really combat racism and all forms of prejudice is to learn to love each other. This is a very important message, which I think is very relevant to now.

Nicholas Boggs has spent 20 or so years writing this biography. It’s an extraordinary labour of love: with lots of new original research, letters that hadn’t been seen before, and so on. It’s a super interesting life.

Let’s go on to Days of Love and Rage: A Story of Revolution by Anand Gopal. This is about the Syrian uprising of 2011, although it starts a bit before.

There are so many stories in this book. It’s so moving and tragic and sad, but it’s very readable. Anand Gopal takes us through a very complicated historical event. He starts in the years just before the Arab Spring and takes us through the Syrian civil war by telling the stories of this diverse group of ordinary Syrians living in a town called Manbij.

You get to know the characters—about their childhood, who they fall in love with, who their parents are. Then they come together at a certain point and carry out an experiment in democracy. They’re trying to figure out how to run their town: who is going to collect the rubbish, who is going to police it. They fall out and have arguments and the war carries on. Then ISIS comes into town as well. You experience all this through these characters.

I’m a big fan of the great American reporter Martha Gellhorn, who reported from the Spanish Civil War. She always argued that her form of reporting was a view from the ground, not from the elites or the great men. It was about how ordinary people went through conflict, and this book is a really good example.

In their review, the New York Times compared this book to Orwell’s Homage to Catalonia. You have the euphoria of revolution, and then you have the collapse, the sense of betrayal when it fails.

You really feel for the people, the individual stories. I’m reading this book again now, and thinking about the lack of empathy we have for people escaping from conflict zones. When you read a book like this, you really understand people’s lives in minute detail and what they’ve had to go through and why they might be compelled to flee their country.

On a wider scale, I think the book makes some interesting points about revolution: you see parallels with the French Revolution and the Russian Revolution. It’s this desire for people living under autocracy to rule themselves, to have some say, some control over their lives, but, sadly, this experiment ends in terrible violence.

It’s an extraordinary piece of reporting. Anand Gopal writes for the New Yorker. He heard about this town, Manbij, and went there in 2017 to report on it. By then, they’re very suspicious. They don’t really want to talk to an American of all people. America’s let them down. There are lots of places in the book where they really hope the Americans will come and save them, and of course they never come—despite Obama’s red lines.

So what Gopal does is he recruits some of the participants in the story, and he says, ‘Okay, you record your friends.’ There are something like 2000 interviews and hours and hours of tape, which he weaves together into this extraordinary piece of narrative writing. It’s like a jigsaw puzzle, or some beautifully woven tapestry.

Now we’ve got a book which is set closer to home. This is London Falling by Patrick Radden Keefe. He’s another very good writer who has won the Baillie Gifford Prize before for his book about the opioid crisis, Empire of Pain. What’s the story he’s telling in this book?

This is a compelling narrative about the tragic death of a London teenager, Zac Brettler. After his death, his parents found out he had been leading a double life, posing as a Russian oligarch’s son. Possibly he’d been inspired by the wealthy children around him at a very expensive North London private school, or it could have been things he saw online, but he wanted that lifestyle.

A lot of young people are reading this book, and it is quite a publishing phenomenon in terms of the demographics it’s reaching. I asked my 25-year-old goddaughter why she liked it, and she said it’s because she comes from a generation where they’re used to people leading double or alternative lives online. The fact that he wanted that life with a fancy car, pretending that he lived in a really expensive apartment building, is all part of the influencer culture.

As a parent, anybody who’s ever had teenagers will relate to this book. How well do you know your teenager? How much do you know about what they’re doing? Then there is the guilt when you find out you had no idea.

What I also really liked about the book is that Radden Keefe then zooms out and produces a portrait of London, a city which has been completely transformed in the course of my lifetime. Starting with the Big Bang and deregulation of the money markets in the 1980s, huge wealth came into London. Some of it was legitimate, some of it illegitimate. It became a magnet for foreign money. That lifted the city and, in many ways, it is a richer and more attractive city than it was. But it also brought in some pretty unpleasant people.

As well as being this tragic, personal story, the book is almost like a thriller involving Russian money and international crime. It’s also a book about personal secrets. There are quite a lot of secrets being held, not least by Zac’s grandfather, who also had a secret life.

It’s a page-turner, a jolly good read. Patrick Radden Keefe brought his outsider’s eye to the troubles in Northern Ireland with his book Say Nothing, and I think he’s done it again with London in London Falling.

Is it the story of a corrupt London?

Yes. It’s an almost Dickensian portrait of modern London because you’ve got all these extraordinary characters in it. It’s about the dark underbelly of the city, which this kid gets drawn into through his lies.

You also have this interweaving between respectable London society, people who have got wealthy in legitimate ways, and people who haven’t. Unfortunately Zac, by pretending to be a Russian oligarch’s son, was targeted by some criminals who thought he was a rich boy, and then got very angry when they found out he wasn’t.

Okay, we’re now at the fifth book on the shortlist. It’s called The Great Dictator: A Life of Barbara Cartland by Matthew Sweet. Could you maybe start by telling us who Barbara Cartland was?

Barbara Cartland was probably the most prolific romantic novelist ever. She wrote 723 books, and the reason this biography is called The Great Dictator is that she dictated most of them.

Most people in Britain of a certain age know who Barbara Cartland was because she was a larger-than-life character. She was this extraordinary figure who always dressed in pink, usually pink taffeta. She had these unbelievably long black false eyelashes, which she coated with boot polish because she thought that was more effective than mascara. She was always pictured on a chaise longue, surrounded by small white fluffy Pekinese dogs, and that’s how she dictated her books.

What attracted us to the book was that it’s also a compelling piece of social history. Barbara Cartland lived from 1901 to 2000, so her life maps onto the 20th century. It’s a very British story, and it tells you a lot about the British class system. She was born into a quite upper-class Edwardian family, but they lost their money. You could say that Barbara was driven, for the rest of her life, by wanting to recoup that wealth.

She comes of age in the Roaring Twenties and is one of the bright young things immortalised by Evelyn Waugh. That’s when she’s coming out and trying to find a husband, but the men of her generation have fought in the trenches and are traumatised by the First World War.

She has two younger brothers, who she loses in the Second World War. One of them was a Conservative MP. Barbara Cartland was very anti-Nazi in the 1930s, at a time when a lot of her class were not. That was partly the influence of her younger brother, who was a friend of Churchill, and was arguing at the time of appeasement that we needed to be more wary of Hitler.

The other thing that really impressed us was that it would be really easy for Matthew Sweet, as a writer, to make fun of her, but he doesn’t. It’s funny—don’t get me wrong—because she’s an inherently comical figure in some ways. But he treats her with respect. She’s an outrageous snob, but he doesn’t need to tell you that. He’s showing, not telling, and I think that’s important in nonfiction: I hate to be told what to think about somebody.

He paints this very vivid portrait of her. She was a very paradoxical person. Every single book she wrote followed pretty much the same template: a woman falls in love with a man, and then immediately becomes a good wife and gives up working. Barbara Cartland didn’t really believe that women should work, so whenever she was interviewed and asked about her work, she said, ‘I’m not a working woman. I’m just writing stories.’ But she was the main breadwinner and very active in the war. After the war, she became a local councillor. She was a busy lady, and not one who was happy to sit at home raising the kids. She wanted to get out there, but that contradicted her romantic ideas.

You feel slightly sorry for her oldest daughter, Raine. Most British people will know that Raine married not just one member of the aristocracy, but three—the final husband being Princess Diana’s father. So she was Lady Spencer, immortalised in the papers as ‘Acid Raine’ by her stepchildren. Reading this book, you feel Raine is almost like an experiment for her mother. She tells her off for being too clever at school. She’s always telling Raine she needs to be attractive to men. She’s expected to marry well, and that means money and a title. She’s almost creating one of these characters in the book.

And is Barbara Cartland a dictator in both senses of the word—was she incredibly bossy?

She was incredibly bossy, but I think ‘the great dictator’ refers to the fact that she dictated her books and she was unbelievably prolific. She had 723 books published, and then Matthew Sweet is given access to her house and finds she’s written about another 100 unpublished books.

It’s impressive, even if the plots and characters are formulaic.

They sold in the millions. Women bought these books. They provided escapism. I’ve got a South African brother-in-law who grew up in a township where there were very few books. His mother was a cleaner, and she used to bring back books from other people’s houses, so he read Barbara Cartland when he was young in South Africa.

Finally, we have another biography: The Traveller: The Revolutionary Life of George Forster and his Search for Humanity by Andrea Wulf.

I love this book. It’s about a forgotten figure from history, George Forster (1754-1794). He was an explorer and an anthropologist. As a 17-year-old, he went on Captain Cook’s second voyage, and Wulf explains in the book that she actually goes to these places—the southern tip of New Zealand, the South Pacific. She travels in Forster’s footsteps, and it’s this really vivid, immersive piece of writing.

Then there is her research. Wulf has access to the German archives—his letters and his diaries. Forster was himself a very good writer. In fact, he wrote up the Captain Cook voyage, and it was a bestselling travel book in the 18th century.  He was quite famous, travelling round Europe, and being invited to courts to tell his stories.

What made him quite special was that, unlike most Europeans at that time, he did not see the indigenous peoples that he encountered on the Cook voyage as inferior in any way. He saw them as equals. At that time, most Europeans assumed that they were superior and were bringing civilization to these places, but he was a humanist. He saw them as members of society that had evolved differently from Europeans, and made a real effort to learn their languages and their customs.

He went on to have a really interesting life. He became an academic in various European universities. He was also a feminist. He married a woman who treated him appallingly. They had an open marriage and she had all these affairs. He didn’t have affairs, but felt she needed the freedom to express herself.

He also has this awful father who is a botanist and takes him across Catherine the Great’s Russia as a child. I think that’s where the empathy comes from. If, at age ten, you’re dragged across Russia for several years, then you go to London in your teens and have to learn English—and are completely self-taught—then, at age 17, you go on Captain Cook’s voyage, you learn to see different perspectives. At a time when most people grow up in their village and never leave it, his knowledge of the world was extraordinary at a very young age.

Finally, at the end of the century, he becomes a revolutionary and moves to Paris. He takes part in the French Revolution, which, inevitably, he sees descend into terror, and he dies a very disappointed man.

So it’s an incredible life. She’s a beautiful writer.

It sounds like an extraordinary window into the 18th century.

Absolutely. It’s a story of the Enlightenment as well. Wulf has written a lot about the 18th century—she has a book about Alexander von Humboldt, The Invention of Nature. Her last book, Magnificent Rebels, was about the German Romantics. It was a really interesting period.

Thank you so much for introducing these books. It’s a great range of books on the shortlist this year. Was it hard getting it down to just six?

This year was a very strong year for non-fiction, so it was very tough coming up with the shortlist. I’m proud of it because it is very varied. To have a list that includes Barbara Cartland and the Syrian Revolution, as well as Alexander the Great, is quite an achievement.

They’re very rich books. I’ve really enjoyed reading all of them.

Five Books aims to keep its book recommendations and interviews up to date. If you are the interviewee and would like to update your choice of books (or even just what you say about them) please email us at [email protected]

Five Books interviews are expensive to produce. If you've enjoyed this interview, please support us by donating a small amount.

entries.title: The best books on Medieval Europe, recommended by Thomas Williams
entries.summary: Europe experienced huge cultural, social and religious change throughout the Middle Ages. You may know it as an age of kings and queens, castles, crusades and chivalric knighthoods, but historians of the period often neglect the seismic events of the far north and east, explains Thomas Williams. Here, he recommends five books that may upend your understanding of medieval Europe. This interview app
entries.content:
Europe experienced huge cultural, social and religious change throughout the Middle Ages. You may know it as an age of kings and queens, castles, crusades and chivalric knighthoods, but historians of the period often neglect the seismic events of the far north and east, explains Thomas Williams. Here, he recommends five books that may upend your understanding of medieval Europe.

Let’s start by defining our terms. When do you consider the medieval period in Europe to have begun, and when did it end?

It’s not a straightforward question, particularly for someone like me, an early medievalist. My idea of the early Middle Ages probably begins somewhat before many other people’s. There’s a popular conception of the Middle Ages as the period from the Norman Conquest onwards: the period of knights, castles, crusades and all the rest of that business.

But for me, if you want to define the medieval period as something in the west of Europe that is post-imperial, but with structured kingship and the institutional presence of the Christian Church, then I think the sixth century is probably the earliest you can reasonably go. But it’s probably not until the seventh century that it starts to look recognisably ‘medieval’.

There is also the complicating factor of what is sometimes called ‘Late Antiquity’, which doesn’t have any hard-and-fast boundaries, but is sometimes imagined to run from the late third to the seventh century.

In terms of the end-point, we’re imprisoned a little bit by Anglophone historiography, which likes to think in terms of the Reformation and Henry VIII’s break with Rome. Obviously, things can feel very different depending on where you’re standing in Europe. But I think the Reformation is still probably the conventional endpoint.

When it comes to my own geographical areas of interest, you could look at something like the collapse of the Teutonic Order in the Baltic, which is broadly speaking part of the Reformation. The secularisation of the Prussian branch of the Teutonic Order occurs in 1525, and that’s an interesting moment. It’s a watershed, where a very distinctive theocratic monastic state, so bound up with ideas and institutions we think of as definitively medieval, breaks down and becomes secularised and Protestant. In Livonia, where the Catholic Order persists, the geopolitics change in the mid-sixteenth century; you suddenly have the Russians under Ivan IV (‘the Terrible’) making land grabs into the Baltic and effectively destroying what remains of the monastic state; it feels like a very different world.

So, yes, this doesn’t nail it down, does it? But very broadly speaking, those would be my parameters. You could pick any number of things, couldn’t you? I suppose the fall of Constantinople to the Turks in 1453 is another contender, but we’re in the right sort of ballpark with the sixteenth century.

I suppose any of these sweeping demarcations have to be, to some extent, artificial. Retrospectively imposing an imaginary framework upon a messy past.

Absolutely. This really gets to the heart of what I’ve been trying to do with my book. It looks at two chapters of medieval history, or what are often seen as distinct chapters: the Viking Age, which in the popular imagination is a time of pagan gods, longships and axe-wielding barbarians, and the age of the Crusades, which is popularly a time of knights, castles, piety and holy war.

They sit very separately, at least from the English perspective, which situates the Norman Conquest right in the middle as a dividing line, with this absurd notion that the Viking Age ended with the death of Harald Hardrada on the battlefield at Stamford Bridge in 1066.

Being familiar with both sides of the divide, it struck me quite forcibly that this is a very false picture, because they bleed into each other in profound ways. The Viking Age doesn’t just stop; it carries on in different forms, with different language and different objectives. But strands and themes carry through deep into the High Middle Ages – longships being one – and things we associate with the High Middle Ages are found in the Viking Age as well: Christian kingship, ideas about holy war, that strange combination of faith and belligerence. So one is in conversation with the other.

Yes. It’s interesting to see how your recommended authors have chosen to organise or bracket their own work. Would you talk through how you made this selection of five books—what you were thinking about?

Well, it was an interesting conundrum. Medieval Europe is a vast subject, spanning an enormous chronological and geographical range. Inevitably, I was looking for books that spoke to my own interests and field of research, but which also said something broader about Europe through that lens.

I knew I couldn’t attempt complete coverage, or I’d be getting into what’s going on in Iberia and the Holy Roman Empire and agricultural change and social transformations and architectural history and goodness knows what else. It would become a fruitless exercise in trying to hit all the bases. So I wanted to find a route that came from a particular perspective. The list reflects my research interests, but also my professional career trajectory and how I’ve arrived at my understanding of Europe.

It was hugely influential because it foregrounded the idea that there is nothing inevitable about Europe as we find it today, or about how it developed in the Middle Ages. Europe was constructed rather than simply coming into being.

In some ways, that feels obvious now, because a lot of work has built on Bartlett’s ideas or challenged them in different ways. But at the time it was published, the notion that Europe was itself a product of colonial expansion, rather than just an exporter of colonial mentalities, was quite radical.

I think that was very persuasive, although parts of it are open to challenge. I would say that Bartlett doesn’t always give due weight to the contingencies around this narrative. The shape of the Europe that emerged was the product of a series of accidents and circumstances that could have turned out differently. Much of the way Europe expanded – north, south, east and west – was also the product of complicated negotiations with other peoples, cultures and ideas, and of the transformations that resulted. It wasn’t entirely a process of erasure and replacement. So there are nuances to the model that I would suggest are valuable to keep in mind. But broadly speaking, it is compelling. Europe was made, it was not inevitable.

Did you meet with this book early in your specialisation?

Not particularly. My background is primarily as an early medievalist, and much of my training was archaeological. I came to the High Middle Ages, and the later Middle Ages, as an extension of previous work I’d done on the Viking Age, which was itself an extension of my work on the even earlier Middle Ages.

I first read this perhaps ten or fifteen years ago, which doesn’t seem that long ago to me. Long enough, I suppose, but it wasn’t formative in my journey, if that’s what you mean. Many of the things it touches on—the Northern Crusades in particular, which form a main plank of his argument about the expansion of Europe’s northeastern frontiers—were subjects I first encountered as an undergraduate.

I had one lecture on the Northern Crusades, and I remember being stunned by it because it was the first time I’d ever encountered this history and I found it mind-blowing. The story of the pagan temple at Arkona and its destruction by the Danes in 1168; the fact that there were still pagans in the Baltic in the late fourteenth century using black powder weapons against the knights of the Teutonic Order; or that Henry Bolingbroke (the future Henry IV) led an army to besiege Vilnius in 1390. This stuff really stayed with me.

I’ve continued to keep abreast of the subject, and writing God’s Hammer was an opportunity to bring a lot of those interests into the book and into conversation with things I’d already studied in more detail. So Bartlett has been in the background for me, but I also find his work interesting because of the broader resonances. He’s talking about the High Middle Ages, but his account of the aggressive manner in which the Roman Church pushed its exclusive message through the conversion period can be applied to the Viking Age and to the seventh-century conversion of the Anglo-Saxons. You can also see it operating within Francia in the sixth century, and you can trace the origins of the process even further back.

Your book God’s Hammer is subtitled ‘A History of the Viking Crusades’. Could you say more about that?

The title is deliberately provocative, because the idea of a Viking ‘crusade’ will feel counterintuitive to most people. There are two things going on here. One is the fact that Scandinavians participated in and led formal crusades, both to the Holy Land and in the Baltic, from the beginning of the twelfth century (towards the end of what would traditionally be seen as the Viking period), into the thirteenth century and beyond.

So there’s that side of the equation: definite Scandinavian involvement in the crusading movement. How ‘Viking’ that was is one question that the book seeks to answer.

The other side of it is that you have what I would call ‘holy wars’ or proto-crusades: aggressive wars of conversion waged by Christian kings long before the First Crusade got underway. You see this very strongly in seventh-century England, in the Frankish world with Clovis and Charlemagne and – most importantly for my book – in Viking Age Scandinavia, where a very aggressive push to Christianise the Scandinavian regions began in the tenth century, bound up with a drive to establish a more dominant model of kingship, a specifically Christian model of kingship.

All of this arguably stretches right back to Constantine at the Milvian Bridge, a foundational narrative for the idea of muscular Christian kingship, wrapped up in Christian symbolism. I’m particularly interested in how those ideas were packaged to appeal to the pagan societies of the north, and what the results of that were.

So I’m coming at this from both ends, which I think is fairly unusual. Not many books have tried to take that long view, and certainly not from a Scandinavian perspective.

Thank you so much. You stay with the Vikings for your next book recommendation, which is Vikings: Life and Legend, a book published in 2014 that offers an overview of the Vikings’ incredible influence.

This is the book associated with the British Museum exhibition in 2014. I joined the project in 2013 as project curator, and – although I can’t claim credit for the intellectual formation of the exhibition; the book had already been written by the time I joined the team – I laid a lot of the groundwork for the show, working with the objects, writing text for the exhibition itself and developing and delivering the public programme.

The bigger argument the exhibition was making was that we shouldn’t see the Vikings as an isolated phenomenon affecting Britain and parts of western Europe: a walk-on part in history, or a disruptive event that arrived like a spell of bad weather. In truth the Viking world had an enormous footprint. Through their maritime culture, the Vikings became the first people to reach four continents. They forged communication networks and effected cultural transformations that had a profound impact on the trajectory of Europe. They shaped the political destiny of multiple European nations: England, Scotland, Ireland, France, Russia and Ukraine among them. The exhibition was giving the Vikings back some of their dignity, agency and transformative power in the European story.

That’s hugely important for how we understand the medieval world as an interconnected whole, rather than a collection of isolated national stories.

This is an interesting one. It doesn’t specifically address the medieval world as it was, but rather how our idea of it—and, specifically, of the Vikings—is largely a product of the nineteenth century. It’s a creation of Victorian scholarship, even down to the popularisation of ‘Viking’ as the term for these people. Before the Victorians, they had been called ‘Danes’ or ‘heathens’, and sometimes Norsemen. There was no fixed way of describing them, and then ‘Viking’ emerged as a preferred term in that period, for better or worse.

The ‘Vikings’ were a Victorian creation, and the implications are huge, because the Victorians also brought assumptions about race, heredity, empire and the superiority of the Germanic world. Those assumptions had implications for how Britain saw itself and how its role as a Christian empire was perceived.

There’s a massive amount of baggage bound up with the creation and perpetuation of these ideas. Again, it gets me into this business of not wanting to accept the categories and boundaries established through historiographical convention.

This has implications for the whole medieval period and for medieval Europe as an entity: what defines Europe, what defines Christianity, what defines paganism, and so on. When you start to peel back the layers of the onion, you can quite swiftly find that you’re looking at a nineteenth-century antiquarian construction founded on little more than late-imperial prejudices about the world in which its creators lived.

It’s a very useful prompt for readers, to remind them to think critically about perceived wisdom. I’ll keep us moving: next we have Christian Raffensperger’s Reimagining Europe: Kievan Rus’ in the Medieval World. This is a topic I’m not familiar with at all—could you introduce me?

Yes. This is helpful I think because it sits in a useful conversation with Bartlett’s book. It’s not a direct corrective, but a complicating factor. What Raffensperger is essentially saying is that we tend to look at Europe as a western-European-centric entity that expands into a sort of ‘outland’: the amorphous world beyond Frankish Latin Christendom.

Raffensperger argues that, if you look at it from an Eastern European perspective, you find yourself in a highly developed, sophisticated Greek-Christian world, both in Byzantium and in Kyivan Rūs – the precursor state, if you like, to modern Russia, Belarus and Ukraine.

His core argument is that if you strip away preconceived notions of what Europe is, you find that Rūs, as it was then constituted, had much deeper connections with western Europe and was more important in terms of its diplomatic, economic and outward-facing connections than we tend to assume. It should really be thought of as a Christian European power, no different from medieval France, the Holy Roman Empire or England. It’s an attempt to reframe what we mean by Europe.

If you think about Bartlett’s argument, his perspective is of a western Frankish Christendom that is expanding outwards towards the east. Well, yes, it is, but it is meeting something equally sophisticated, equally Christian and equally vibrant. It’s only historical accident, in the shape of the Mongol invasions, that really scrambles that map. We don’t know what Europe would look like had it not been for the disruption of southern routes to the Black Sea in the thirteenth century, or for that matter the sack of Constantinople by the Crusaders in 1204. These were historical moments with huge transformative effects. We don’t have a counterfactual for what Europe might otherwise have become.

What’s coming through in your book recommendations is an invigorating sense of destabilisation. They call into question everything we think of when we think of medieval Europe, right?

Yes, I like that! I think that’s one of the reasons I’ve been drawn to these writers and books. As God’s Hammer probably implies, I’m interested in the collision of worlds: what happens in those interactions, what are the messy crossovers, and where are the moments of contingency on which so much of this history hangs. Are we looking at things clearly? Are we standing far enough away to get the proper picture? Or are we enmeshed in modern, preconceived visions? All these books address that in different ways.

This is the newest book on the list. It only came out this year, and it’s a wonderful book. It sets out in clear and logical detail a subject that is woefully undertaught, misunderstood and, frankly, not even known about by many: despite the fact that these crusades fundamentally transformed the boundaries of Europe in ways that other crusading movements spectacularly failed to accomplish.

A lot of people studying medieval history would be astounded to learn that Scottish crusaders travelled to fight holy wars in the frozen forests of Lithuania, or that the biggest castle in Europe – Malbork in Poland – was built as the headquarters of the Teutonic Order in former East Prussia. These are bonkers narratives if you’ve never encountered them before. The landscape and climate give the whole thing an amazing cinematic quality, with its wilderness and snow. It’s quite a wonderful story.

Crucially, Pluskowski’s book fundamentally updates the previous history of the subject, Eric Christiansen’s The Northern Crusades, published in 1997. That’s also a great book and one that had a great influence on me personally. But it’s also nearly thirty years old, and there has been a huge amount of archaeological work on the northern Crusades that has been conducted in the last fifteen or twenty years, much of it led by Aleksander himself.

I actually dug with him for a season in eastern Poland, in Masuria. His work produced a massive amount of environmental data that show how the Crusades transformed the physical landscape, patterns of land-use and biodiversity in the region, as well as the physical castles and churches built by the Teutonic Knights and others during their conquests, and the cultural and religious changes experienced by people in material terms. The Black Cross draws on all of this new work as well as the medieval chronicles of the period to really enrich understanding of the period. So a big thumbs-up for that.

Thank you, and it’s great to have a sense of spread in the book choices—we have books from several decades ago coming right up into the present. As a closing question, do you have any other suggestions to offer readers seeking to expand their understanding of the medieval world?

I’d emphasise a couple of things I’ve already mentioned. Any approach to the Middle Ages risks getting bogged down in older scholarship that brings a lot of inherited baggage with it. People should be alert to that: always challenge the assumption on the page.

The other thing I’d say, if people are really interested in this stuff, is to go back to the primary sources. It’s all very well reading a secondary work that retells a historical narrative, but you’re effectively reading another layer of interpretation, which colours the framing of the history it’s trying to tell. If you go to the primary record, you can see what the chronicler was actually trying to say in their own words. Of course, we’re often dealing with translations, so it’s not completely straightforward. But it’s one of the easiest ways to cut through a lot of that accumulated historiographical or cultural baggage.

It’s particularly important at the moment because the Middle Ages is where a lot of ethnonationalist narratives draw their sustenance. If those narratives aren’t challenged, or if people aren’t looking at the actual sources on which they’re supposedly based, they’re going to be easily misled. It happens all the time.

Thomas Williams is a historian and archaeologist and the author of Viking Britain, Viking London and Lost Realms. He was project curator of the British Museum’s major international exhibition Vikings: Life and Legend(2014), and later curated the museum's early medieval coin collection. He holds a PhD from UCL and is a Fellow of the Society of Antiquaries and Royal Historical Society. His new book God's Hammer: a History of the Viking Crusades is out now.

entries.content:
We love books about ancient history at Five Books. Not only is it relaxing to escape from the present by reading about events several millennia ago, but the brutality of that period also helps put our modern challenges in perspective. One exciting trend in the past few years is a move away from accounts of ancient Rome and Greece to other ancient civilisations. Here's a roundup of some of the books published recently.

A really immersive book that makes it hard not to pack your bags and head to Tunisia is Carthage: A New History of an Ancient Empire by Eve MacDonald, a classicist and archaeologist who teaches at Cardiff University:

The Library of Ancient Wisdom, a book by Assyriologist Selena Wisnom, takes us to Iraq in the 7th century BCE and the library of Ashurbanipal. It’s been shortlisted for the Wolfson Prize, the UK’s most prestigious history prize:

Staying in Mesopotamia, our contributing editor Tuva Kahrs also really enjoyed Between Two Rivers and the way it’s concerned with people’s lives. “I particularly loved the description of bricks with dog paw prints and clay writing tablets with children’s fingerprints from thousands of years ago,” she writes. She interviewed the author, Moudhy Al-Rashid, on the best books about Mesopotamia.

We spoke to historian Lloyd Llewellyn-Jones about the Persian Empire a few years ago. He’s now written a book on Babylon, ‘the mother of all cities.’ Given how it’s been vilified in the Biblical tradition, it’s quite fun to read a book that puts the record straight. “The Babylon you will meet in this book was a thriving, rich and advanced ancient Near Eastern city with a singular identity, which it maintained for well over 2000 years,” he writes.

We’re fans of books by Robert Harris at Five Books, as his historical fiction tends to be based on primary sources, and it’s a relaxing way to learn about history. Agrippa is about Augustus’s best friend and presents him as the genius behind the military victories that enabled Octavian, the great-nephew of Julius Caesar, to become the first Roman emperor.

Also recently recommended on Five Books in historical fiction is Boudicca’s Daughter by Elodie Harper. Set in Britain at the time of the Roman invasion, it’s about the daughter of the late Iron Age queen, Boudicca. According to Alex Bescoby, one of the judges of the Wilbur Smith Adventure Writing Prize, the book is realistic, in as much as it can be “about a culture that was essentially eradicated and happened a very long time ago. There’s not a lot to work from, but I found the story compelling.” (We also have nonfiction book recommendations about Boudicca, by Richard Hingley, a professor of Archaeology at Durham University).

October 30, 2026
